introduction: From exile and prison Bahá’u’lláh wrote to the rulers of his age, to the Shah, the Sultan, Napoleon III, Queen Victoria, the Czar and others, and to kings as a body, calling them to justice, to care for the poor, to peace, and to recognize the one who addressed them. The Báb had written to the Shah before him. These passages give the summons, tell how the letters were carried and received, and record what was foretold for those who refused. Sixty-nine outside voices stand beside them: Moses before Pharaoh, Nathan and Daniel before kings, the Psalms and Proverbs on thrones, the Qur’an's letter from Solomon, Muḥammad's letter to Heraclius, Confucius and Mencius counselling rulers, and Sophocles, Shakespeare and Shelley, with Thucydides and Machiavelli speaking for power as it is.
questions: What do these summonses ask of a ruler, and how does it compare with what Proverbs, Deuteronomy and Confucius ask?
Moses was told to speak gently to Pharaoh; Nathan trapped David with a story; Daniel read out a sentence. Which manners of address do you find in these letters?
A talk remarks that Christ wrote to neither Herod nor Pilate. Why might one messenger address the powerful directly and another not?
Thucydides' Athenians and Machiavelli describe how power behaves. What claim do letters from a prisoner make against that description?
Several passages say that what was foretold for certain rulers came to pass. How should such fulfilments be weighed, with Ozymandias and the Qur’an's abandoned gardens in mind?
"Blessed is the king who hath cast away kingship." What would it mean for anyone who holds authority to hear these letters as addressed to them?

outside.why: The second psalm addresses kings in the same voice: be wise now, O ye kings; be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Proverbs says that wickedness is an abomination in kings, since a throne is established by righteousness.
Shakespeare's Portia says that mercy becomes a throned monarch better than his crown.
Machiavelli advised princes that it is safer to be feared than loved. What does a crown of justice ask of a ruler that his counsel does not?
Jeremiah asks a king whether he reigns because he lives in cedar, and reminds him that his father judged the cause of the poor.
A king's mother in Proverbs teaches him to open his mouth for the dumb and plead the cause of the poor.
Mencius ranked the people first in a nation and the sovereign last.
Paul writes from his chains that the word of God is not bound.
Machiavelli noted that armed prophets conquer and unarmed prophets are destroyed. What kind of sovereignty is claimed by a prisoner writing to kings?
Mencius, received by a king who hoped for profit, answered that he brought only counsels of benevolence and righteousness.
Moses and Aaron stood before Pharaoh with a message that began "Thus saith the Lord," and Pharaoh asked who the Lord was.
The Qur’an commands those who judge between people to judge justly and to restore what is entrusted to them.
Antigone tells a king that his decrees cannot override the unwritten and unfailing statutes of heaven.
Deuteronomy requires a king to copy out the law and read it all his life, so that his heart is not lifted above his brothers.
Samuel warned a people asking for a king what kings take: their fields, their flocks, themselves. Do these addresses assume that kingship can be made just, or do they share his doubt?
Isaiah cries woe on those who decree unrighteous decrees and take away the right of the poor.
Ezekiel arraigns the shepherds of his people for feeding themselves and not the flock.
Victor Hugo, in the same decades, told a peace congress that a day would come when the nations of Europe would lay down their arms.
Paul tells the Philippians that his chains have served to advance his message, even in the palace.
The Chronicler tells of rulers who mocked the messengers sent to them until there was no remedy.
Ahab greeted Elijah as the troubler of Israel, and was told that the trouble was his own doing.
The Qur’an tells David that he has been made a viceroy on earth and must judge rightly, for there is a day of reckoning.
A psalm prays that the king be given God's judgments, so that he may judge the poor with justice.
The Qur’an tells of a letter from Solomon to the Queen of Sheba, opening in the name of God and calling her to come in submission.
Moses and Aaron were told to speak a gentle word to Pharaoh, in case he might heed. This letter to the Shah is courteous, others are severe. When is each manner right?
Paul, in chains before King Agrippa, wished the king to be as he was, except for the bonds.
Jesus told his disciples that they would be brought before governors and kings to bear witness.
Moses was sent to Pharaoh with a message in God's name and a warning of what refusal would cost.
Stephen, the first to die for delivering his message, died praying for those who killed him.
John the Baptist told Herod what was not lawful for him, and Herod feared him, heard him gladly and had him killed.
Muḥammad wrote in the same way to the emperor Heraclius, in the name of God, inviting him.
Jesus, struck at his hearing, asked his accusers to state the wrong he had done.
The Preacher says that a poor and wise child is better than an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished.
Nathan also tested a king with a story before he told him: thou art the man.
Daniel read to a king the writing on his wall: weighed in the balances and found wanting.
When Jonah's warning reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne and sat in ashes, and the city was spared. What would that have looked like in a nineteenth-century court?
The Preacher, a king in Jerusalem, looked on all his works and found them vanity.
Daniel tells how a voice from heaven announced to a king at the height of his pride that the kingdom had departed from him.
Amos asks that judgment run down as waters and righteousness as a mighty stream.
The neighbours of Jesus saw only the carpenter's son among them, and were offended at him.
Paul said of the chains awaiting him that none of these things moved him, if he might finish his course.
The second psalm pictures the kings of the earth setting themselves against the Lord, who is not moved.
Jesus told his disciples to proclaim on the housetops what they had heard in the ear.
Amos explained why he spoke to the powerful: the Lord God has spoken; who can but prophesy?
The Athenian envoys in Thucydides say that right is in question only between equals, and that otherwise the strong do what they can. What answer do these summonses make to that view?
Jesus told Pilate that he would have no power at all unless it were given from above.
Jesus told Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world, and wrote to no ruler. Why might one messenger address the kings and another stand silent before them?
Plato thought cities would have no rest from evils until philosophers were kings, or kings philosophers. Are kings here asked to become wise, or to obey?
Proverbs says that it is the honour of kings to search out a matter.
David, a king, prays: thine is the kingdom, O Lord, and thou art exalted as head above all.
Shakespeare's sleepless king envies the poor their rest: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
Shakespeare's Richard says that within the hollow crown of a king Death keeps his court.
Jefferson wrote that he trembled for his country when he reflected that God is just.
Acton judged that power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely. Is the preoccupation described here a fault of particular rulers or of power itself?
The Qur’an says of Pharaoh's people: how many gardens and springs they left behind, an inheritance for others.
Shelley's king of kings survives as a boast on a broken statue in an empty desert.
Hamlet reflects that imperious Caesar, dead and turned to clay, might stop a hole to keep the wind away.
Gray's elegy says that the paths of glory lead but to the grave.
Daniel blesses the God who changes the times and removes kings and sets up kings.
Isaiah says that God brings princes to nothing and blows on them so that they wither.
The Qur’an addresses God as the owner of sovereignty, who gives it and withdraws it as he will.
Mary sings of a God who has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble.
A psalm warns against trust in princes, whose plans perish with their breath.
The Qur’an says that Pharaoh's body was saved from the sea as a sign for those who came after.
Jesus asks what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Confucius told a ruler that to govern means to rectify, and that if he led with correctness none would dare do otherwise.
Confucius said that the ruler is to the people as wind to grass: the grass bends as the wind blows.
The governor Felix trembled as Paul reasoned of justice and judgment, and sent him away until a more convenient season.
Machiavelli held that a prudent ruler cannot keep faith when it is against his interest. If kings act only for their own benefit, to whom are such letters really addressed?

psalm-be-wise-o-ye-kings.text: Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling

exodus-let-my-people-go.text: And afterward Moses and Aaron went in, and told Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness. And Pharaoh said, Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go

mark-john-and-herod.text: For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife. Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly

acts-almost-thou-persuadest-me.text: King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest. Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds

acts-felix-trembled.text: And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee

matthew-before-governors-and-kings.text: And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles. But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak. For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaketh in you

isaiah-princes-to-nothing.text: That bringeth the princes to nothing; he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity. Yea, they shall not be planted; yea, they shall not be sown: yea, their stock shall not take root in the earth: and he shall also blow upon them, and they shall wither, and the whirlwind shall take them away as stubble

isaiah-unrighteous-decrees.text: Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed; To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless

jeremiah-judged-the-cause-of-the-poor.text: Shalt thou reign, because thou closest thyself in cedar? did not thy father eat and drink, and do judgment and justice, and then it was well with him? He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him: was not this to know me? saith the Lord

proverbs-throne-established-by-righteous.text: It is an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness

proverbs-when-the-wicked-beareth-rule.text: When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn

deuteronomy-king-shall-write-a-copy.text: And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the Lord his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them: That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren

psalm-put-not-your-trust-in-princes.text: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish

daniel-removeth-kings.text: Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever: for wisdom and might are his: And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding

daniel-kingdom-is-departed.text: While the word was in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying, O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will

jonah-king-of-nineveh.text: For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes

ecclesiastes-old-and-foolish-king.text: Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished

chronicles-mocked-the-messengers.text: And the Lord God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place: But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy

samuel-this-will-be-the-manner.text: He will take the tenth of your sheep: and ye shall be his servants. And ye shall cry out in that day

quran-pharaoh-exalted-himself.text: Lo! Pharaoh exalted himself in the earth and made its people castes. A tribe among them he oppressed, killing their sons and sparing their women. Lo! he was of those who work corruption.

quran-judge-justly.text: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners, and, if ye judge between mankind, that ye judge justly. Lo! comely is this which Allah admonisheth you. Lo! Allah is ever Hearer, Seer.

quran-save-thee-in-thy-body.text: But this day We save thee in thy body that thou mayst be a portent for those after thee. Lo! most of mankind are heedless of Our portents.

quran-speak-a-gentle-word.text: Go, both of you, unto Pharaoh. Lo! he hath transgressed (the bounds). And speak unto him a gentle word, that peradventure he may heed or fear

quran-noble-letter.text: O chieftains! Lo! there hath been thrown unto me a noble letter. Lo! it is from Solomon, and lo! it is: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful; Exalt not yourselves against me, but come unto me as those who surrender

quran-how-many-gardens.text: How many were the gardens and the watersprings that they left behind, And the cornlands and the goodly sites And pleasant things wherein they took delight! Even so (it was), and We made it an inheritance for other folk

shakespeare-uneasy-lies-the-head.text: Then happy low, lie down! / Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown
shakespeare-uneasy-lies-the-head.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-hollow-crown.text: for within the hollow crown / That rounds the mortal temples of a king / Keeps Death his court
shakespeare-hollow-crown.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-mercy-becomes-the-monarch.text: 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest: it becomes / The throned monarch better than his crown
shakespeare-mercy-becomes-the-monarch.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

analects-to-govern-is-to-rectify.text: To govern means to rectify. If you lead on the people with correctness, who will dare not to be correct
analects-to-govern-is-to-rectify.author: Confucius

analects-wind-and-grass.text: The relation between superiors and inferiors is like that between the wind and the grass. The grass must bend, when the wind blows across it
analects-wind-and-grass.author: Confucius

sophocles-unwritten-statutes.text: nor deemed I that thy decrees were of such force, that a mortal could override the unwritten and unfailing statutes of heaven
sophocles-unwritten-statutes.author: Sophocles

thucydides-the-strong-do-what-they-can.text: right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must
thucydides-the-strong-do-what-they-can.author: Thucydides

hadith-letter-to-heraclius.text: In the name of Allah the Beneficent, the Merciful (This letter is) from Muhammad the slave of Allah and His Apostle to Heraclius the ruler of Byzantine. Peace be upon him, who follows the right path. Furthermore I invite you to Islam, and if you become a Muslim you will be safe
hadith-letter-to-heraclius.author: Muḥammad

mencius-why-must-your-majesty-say-profit.text: Why must your Majesty use that word "profit?" What I am provided with, are counsels to benevolence and righteousness, and these are my only topics
mencius-why-must-your-majesty-say-profit.author: Mencius

mencius-people-most-important.text: The people are the most important element in a nation; the spirits of the land and grain are the next; the sovereign is the lightest
mencius-people-most-important.author: Mencius
